title: Q1 2026 AI-Hallucination Court Sanctions Cluster — Ringo (Or. Ct. App.), Whiting (6th Cir.), Prososki (Neb.), Sullivan & Cromwell
author: Damien Charlotin · Joe Patrice · Eugene Volokh · ComplianceHub

dom.t: Hallucination governance: Sanctions target inquiry failures

st.t: Litigation responsibility: Sanctions follow conduct and authority
st.an: The source reinforces continuing lawyer accountability and materially extends the synthesis with Ringo’s explicit signature-based false-certification rationale and circumstance-sensitive sanction calibration. Whiting also supports distinguishing clear fabrication and factual misrepresentation from ordinary drafting errors, without assuming AI provenance.

kp.k: Fabricated authorities make signed briefs false certifications
kp.d: In the Oregon Court of Appeals material identified as Ringo, the court treats signing a brief containing fabricated law as a false certification. It regards AI use as the likely source of the fabrications, but explicitly notes that counsel has not directly acknowledged this; AI involvement is therefore a judicial inference rather than an admission.
qs: An attorney who signs a brief supported in full or in part by nonexistent law—law that is fabricated—thus submits a false certification to the court.
Although respondent's counsel has not acknowledged this directly, we recognize the reality that the fabricated law in respondents' brief likely resulted from the use of artificial intelligence.

kp.k: Oregon imposes itemised sanctions for fabricated legal authority
kp.d: The Oregon court sanctions respondents' counsel $500 for each of two fabricated case citations and $1,000 for one fabricated statement of law attributed to an existing case, totalling $2,000. It considers this reasonable for an apparent first occurrence under circumstances suggesting AI involvement. The court struck the brief but permits a replacement supported by existing law.
qs: As described more fully in our show cause order, there are two fabricated case citations, and one fabricated statement of law attributed to an existing case, so we sanction respondents' counsel in the amount of $2,000.

Based on our review of the decisions of other courts, we are persuaded that these sanctions are within the range of what is reasonable for this conduct, at least, where, as here, it appears to be an attorney's first time submitting fabricated authority to the court under circumstances suggesting that artificial intelligence may have played a role.
We allow respondents an opportunity, however, to submit a brief that is supported by existing law.

kp.k: Sanctions address judicial workload and deterrence
kp.d: The Oregon court's survey of 2025 decisions reports monetary responses ranging from a $1,000 penalty or donation to a $10,000 sanction. The quoted rationales include excessive judicial time spent addressing fabricated citations and erroneous legal statements, deterrence of other attorneys, and a jurisdiction-specific penalty ceiling. These are reported court rationales, not measured estimates of AI's aggregate costs.
qs: [a]ttorney Mostafavi's fabricated citations and erroneous statements of law have required this court to spend excessive time on this otherwise straightforward appeal
explaining that the court would impose a $2,500 frivolous motion penalty which is the most the law allows under Court of Appeals Rule 7(e)(2)
will help deter other attorneys from following in Mr. Panichi's footsteps

kp.k: Whiting documents extensive citation and factual misconduct
kp.d: In Whiting v. City of Athens, Tenn., No. 25-5425, dated 13 March 2026, the Sixth Circuit identifies over two dozen fake citations and factual misrepresentations in briefs submitted by Van Irion and Russ Egli. The court calls its count conservative because it excludes typos, sloppy citations, and ambiguous errors. Charlotin's entry separately itemises seven distinct defects; that is not the court's total count. The supplied judicial extracts establish briefing misconduct without expressly confirming its AI origin.
qs: That briefing repeatedly misrepresented the record, cited non-existent cases, and cited cases for propositions of law that they did not even discuss, much less support….
[W]e found over two dozen fake citations and misrepresentations of fact in Whiting's briefs, which we list in an appendix to this opinion.
We do not include typos or sloppy citations.

kp.k: Whiting sanctions include fines, fees, and double costs
kp.d: The document reports, through the Volokh headline and Charlotin's row, opponents' attorney fees, double costs, and a $15,000 fine on each of Whiting's two lawyers, logged as a $30,000 monetary sanction. It also reports dismissal of the appeal as almost entirely frivolous for pervasive misconduct. The $30,000 figure represents the two fines, rather than a stated total including fees and costs.
qs: Outcome per the Volokh headline and Charlotin's row: opponents' attorney fees, double costs, and a $15,000 fine on each of the two lawyers — logged as a $30,000 monetary sanction, with the appeal dismissed as "almost entirely frivolous" for "pervasive misconduct".

kp.k: Firm policies failed to prevent AI citation errors
kp.d: In the April 2026 Prince Global Holdings bankruptcy matter, Sullivan & Cromwell partner Andrew Dietderich acknowledges AI hallucinations in a motion. His letter states that the firm's AI policies were not followed and that its citation-review process failed to identify both AI-generated inaccuracies and other errors apparently attributable wholly or partly to manual error. The account documents a failure to implement safeguards and verify output, rather than an absence of policies or training.
qs: The inaccuracies and errors in the Motion include artificial intelligence ("AI") "hallucinations."
The Firm maintains comprehensive policies and training requirements governing the use of AI tools in legal work.
The Firm's policies on the use of AI were not followed in connection with the preparation of the Motion.
Regrettably, this review process did not identify the inaccurate citations generated by AI, nor did it identify other errors that appear to have resulted in whole or in part from manual error.

kp.k: Correction counts must distinguish hallucinations from other errors
kp.d: Above the Law reports roughly 40 corrections across multiple Sullivan & Cromwell filings, but explicitly distinguishes some citation-style corrections from AI hallucinations. Charlotin's row, dated 2026-04-18, records one fabricated Westlaw citation for Three Arrows Capital, corrected in Schedule A. The document therefore does not support treating all roughly 40 corrections as hallucinations, and it reports no sanction outcome for this matter.
qs: Schedule A to the letter catalogs the damage across the motion, the verified petition, the joint administration motion, the scheduling motion, and a couple of declarations — roughly 40 corrections. Some substantive, some less so, all embarrassing.
It adds that some Schedule A entries are Bluebook-style corrections to Amnesty International and UN human rights report citations, which "aren't AI hallucinations".

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: The source presents concrete incidents of fabricated legal authority entering court filings, exposing lawyers to sanctions and revealing failures of AI-use policies and human verification. It does not offer a general forecast of legal-market transformation.
pts.d: In the Ringo excerpts, the Oregon Court of Appeals attributes fabricated authority to likely, rather than acknowledged or established, AI use. The court states that signing a brief supported by fabricated law constitutes a false certification and imposes personal monetary sanctions. In Whiting, the Sixth Circuit identifies extensive false citations and factual misrepresentations; the compilation reports financial penalties and dismissal, but the supplied court quotations do not expressly establish AI as their cause. For Sullivan & Cromwell, partner Andrew Dietderich explicitly acknowledges AI hallucinations in a motion, noncompliance with the firm's AI policies, and a citation-review process that failed to catch both AI-generated inaccuracies and other errors. These are retrospective claims about litigation practice and accountability, not claims that AI replaces lawyers or changes legal-service pricing.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The evidence consists of judicial findings, reported case outcomes, a law-firm partner's admission, and a correction schedule—not model benchmarks or measured hallucination rates.
pts.d: Ringo identifies two fabricated case citations and one fabricated statement of law, supporting a $2,000 sanction; the court cites other 2025 sanctions decisions to justify the amount. In Whiting, Judge Bush's opinion, joined by Judges Stranch and Murphy, reports over two dozen clear fake citations and factual misrepresentations, excluding mere typos and sloppy citations. The compilation attributes the reported outcome—opponents' attorney fees, double costs, a $15,000 fine for each lawyer, and dismissal—to the Volokh headline and Charlotin's entry. Dietderich's letter supplies direct acknowledgment of AI-related errors at Sullivan & Cromwell. Joe Patrice's Above the Law account reports roughly 40 corrections across several filings, while distinguishing some citation-style corrections from hallucinations. Charlotin's entry records one fabricated Westlaw citation in that matter. Those correction and defect counts are not interchangeable and do not establish a general error rate.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: The claims concern incidents reported in 2026, with 2025 sanctions precedents; their scope is qualified by uncertain AI attribution, first-offense circumstances, and distinctions among types of error.
pts.d: Whiting is dated 13 March 2026. The Sullivan & Cromwell matter is dated April 2026, with Charlotin's entry dated 18 April, so the supplied compilation extends beyond its Q1 title. No precise Ringo decision date is supplied in the body. Ringo expressly limits its assessment of reasonable sanctions to circumstances appearing to involve a first submission of fabricated authority and suggesting AI involvement; it does not announce a universal sanction tariff for all AI errors. Whiting's count covers clearly false citations and misrepresentations, not all drafting mistakes. Dietderich describes safeguards that existed but were not followed, alongside review that failed; he does not claim that all firm AI use produces such failures. The document provides no future adoption or displacement timeline.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The affected parties are filing lawyers, their clients, courts, opposing parties, and law firms responsible for supervision and verification.
pts.d: Ringo imposes $2,000 payable personally by respondents' counsel, strikes the clients' answering brief, and allows a replacement supported by existing law. In Whiting, lawyers Van Irion and Russ Egli face reported individual fines and fee-and-cost consequences, while their client's appeal is dismissed. Courts face additional work identifying and addressing false authority; a 2025 precedent quoted by the Oregon court expressly describes excessive judicial time. Opposing parties are recipients of the reported fee-and-cost award in Whiting. Sullivan & Cromwell must acknowledge and correct errors across multiple bankruptcy filings despite having policies and training. The supplied passage does not report a sanction imposed on that firm, nor does it quantify effects on legal employment, pricing, or access to justice.
